results.title: HYBE targets controlling stake in Japanese agency behind Nogizaka46, SKE48
results.content: HYBE, the K-pop powerhouse behind BTS, is making a major push into Japan's entertainment industry, seeking control of a company behind some of the country's best-known pop acts, including girl groups Nogizaka46 and SKE48, in a deal that could reshape its presence in the world's second-largest recorded music market. HYBE Japan, the Korean entertainment company's Japanese subsidiary, announced Wednesday that it had launched a tender offer for KeyHolder, a Tokyo-listed entertainment company with businesses spanning artist management, television and film production, digital content, advertising and logistics. The offer could give HYBE Japan a controlling stake in KeyHolder, with the maximum investment estimated at 105.7 billion won ($72 million), according to the company's announcement. results.title: N. Korea to hold meeting of grassroots leaders of ruling party this month
results.content: North Korea will hold a meeting of grassroots leaders of the ruling Workers' Party of Korea (WPK) this month to discuss ways to better implement policy goals set forth at a key party congress earlier this year, its state media said Thursday. A conference of the party's "cell secretaries" is scheduled to take place in late November in Pyongyang, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reported. Party cells refer to the party's most elementary units consisting of five to 30 members. The gathering comes as the North has stressed efforts to follow through on its five-year policy goals across a range of sectors, including on the economy and defense, set at the ninth party congress in February. results.title: World Taekwondo marks decade of refugee outreach
results.content: World Taekwondo marked a decade of humanitarian work Wednesday, celebrating its foundation's efforts to bring sporting opportunities to refugee children and young people through taekwondo. The ceremony at Seoul's Olympic Parktel commemorated the 10th anniversary of the Taekwondo Humanitarian Foundation (THF), which was formally established in April 2016 as an independent international nonprofit organization based in Lausanne, Switzerland. The event featured a demonstration by the World Taekwondo Performance Team, remarks by WT President Chungwon Choue, a commemorative concert and an exhibition documenting the foundation's activities. Diplomatic representatives from Croatia, Costa Rica, Uzbekistan, Cambodia, Sri Lanka and Jordan attended the celebration. results.title: UN committee adopts N. Korean human rights resolution for 22nd year
results.content: A U.N. General Assembly committee has passed a resolution on North Korea's human rights situation for the 22nd straight year, expressing concerns over Pyongyang's digital surveillance and technology-enabled repression of its people and other abuses, Seoul's foreign ministry said Thursday. The Third Committee, which handles human rights and social affairs, adopted the resolution with 95 votes in favor, 14 against and 58 abstentions at the U.N. headquarters in New York on Wednesday (local time), sending it to the General Assembly for final approval in December. The United States abstained for the first time, taking issue with a reference in the text to the International Criminal Court (ICC), which Washington has accused of exceeding its jurisdiction and infringing on national sovereignty. results.title: Man behind perfect LEET score vanishes amid AI cheating allegations
results.content: Lee Jin-woo, a person facing allegations of AI cheating on Korea’s law school and college entrance exams, disappeared Thursday morning after failing to show up for a scheduled live "verification test." He had promised to prove his innocence and capability by solving the Korean section of this year's College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT) in real time. Admissions officials said Lee was scheduled to arrive at a testing center in southern Seoul by 8 a.m. But he did not show up. Lee drew scrutiny after surging from low past scores to missing just one question on the last year's CSAT — earning admission to the prestigious Seoul National University’s dental school — and later scoring a perfect mark on the 2027 Legal Education Eligibility Test (LEET). results.title: Seoul shares open higher ahead of Anthropic's market debut
results.content: Seoul shares opened higher Thursday ahead of the stock market debut of U.S. artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic PBC this week amid concerns over the sustainability of AI investments. After opening 0.45 percent higher, the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) rose 6.39 points, or 0.13 percent, to 5,073.83 as of 9:15 a.m. The index ended 1.99 percent higher at 5,067.44 on Wednesday, snapping a four-day losing streak, buoyed by a rally in technology stocks following Nvidia Corp.'s upbeat earnings. Overnight, U.S. stocks closed mixed. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.11 percent, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite rose 0.42 percent. Investors are looking for further evidence that heavy investments in AI will generate sustainable returns as Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI chatbot, is set to make its stock market debut Thursday (U.S. time). results.content: The leaders of the United States, China and Russia were set to hold their first-ever trilateral summit in Shenzhen on Thursday to discuss key international security issues, while uncertainty remains over whether U.S. President Donald Trump will meet North Korean leader Kim Jong-un during his visit to China. Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen later in the day. Trump has expressed his intention to discuss nuclear arms reductions and other major international issues at the three-way summit. The meeting comes amid differences among the three countries over key international issues, including nuclear disarmament and conflicts involving Ukraine and Iran. results.title: Lee, Putin agree to pursue cooperation where possible, work to ease tensions on Korean Peninsula
results.content: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to pursue cooperation where possible while working to ease tensions on the Korean Peninsula, a Seoul official said of their meeting Wednesday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit here in China's Shenzhen. Lee and Putin held a 10-minute meeting after attending a welcome dinner hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping on the first day of the annual APEC leaders' meeting, according to the official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. It marked Lee's first in-person meeting with Putin since taking office in June last year. results.title: Korea's largest game exhibition G-STAR kicks off in Busan
results.content: G-STAR, South Korea's largest game exhibition, kicked off its three-day run on Thursday, bringing together game developers, content creators and fans from around the world in the southern port city of Busan, the event's organizer said. More than 1,200 companies from 41 countries are participating in the event, which runs through Saturday at the BEXCO convention center in the city, some 325 kilometers south of Seoul, the organizer added. Among major game publishers, South Korea's Krafton Inc. is showcasing its flagship and new titles, including PUBG: Battlegrounds, TARAE: The Unbound and Age Twisters. Japan's Sega Corp. is presenting the highly anticipated Total War: Warhammer 40,000 at the trade show, along with other titles, including Crazy Taxi, a driving action game. results.title: NK leader visits naval university, key construction sites amid possible NK-US talks
results.content: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has inspected a naval university and construction sites on the country's eastern coast, state media reported Thursday, amid speculation that U.S. President Donald Trump may meet him in China. Kim visited Kim Jong Suk Naval University and key construction sites in South Hamgyong Province earlier this week, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reported. While inspecting key facilities at the university Wednesday, Kim stressed the importance of maritime defense, saying the "sustained confrontation with the most wicked enemies urgently calls for training more able naval combat system experts and commanding officers proficient at modern warfare," the KCNA said. Kim called on university staff and students to work harder to fulfill their duties in bolstering naval forces. results.title: Korea-China FTA deal on services, investment lays groundwork for deeper economic ties: Cheong Wa Dae
results.content: SHENZHEN, China — A breakthrough in negotiations on services and investment under the Korea-China free trade agreement (FTA) lays the institutional groundwork for deeper economic cooperation between the two countries, presidential chief of staff for policy Ha Joon-kyung said. The two countries announced they had reached a substantive agreement during a summit between President Lee Jae Myung and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Wednesday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China. The breakthrough came eight years and eight months after negotiations began. Speaking at a briefing, Ha said China accounts for a smaller share of Korea’s trade in services than of its trade in goods, leaving considerable room for growth. results.title: 'Can I see my mother?' Korean War veteran recalls American soldier's plea
results.content: PYEONGTAEK, Gyeonggi Province — “Can I see my mother?” More than seven decades later, Korean War veteran Kang Ku-kon still remembers those five words spoken by a young American soldier fighting for his life. The soldier, barely 19, had suffered a severe abdominal wound less than a week after arriving in Korea. Kang, who was helping at a U.S. Army field hospital, was just 15 himself when he went to serve in the 1950-53 Korean War. During a visit to the U.S. Eighth Army headquarters at Camp Humphreys in Pyeongtaek, Gyeonggi Province on Nov. 5, Kang recalled his years with American soldiers. Kang spent part of his childhood in Japan, where his father ran a construction business. He learned to ride horses at an early age but also witnessed American bombing raids during World War II. results.title: Portugal invites Koreans to 2027 Marvão International Music Festival
results.content: The Portugal Embassy in Seoul introduced Korean classical music lovers to the 2027 Marvão International Music Festival, inviting them to experience unique cultural celebration set in one of Portugal's most picturesque destinations. Nestled nearly 800 meters above sea level in the Alentejo region, close to the Spanish border, Marvão is a small medieval village surrounded by stone walls and a castle. Overlooking the vast landscape of the Serra de São Mamede Natural Park, the hilltop town is widely regarded as one of the most beautiful places in Portugal. Once a remote medieval stronghold, Marvão has transformed to an international destination for classical music lovers for summer time since German conductor Christoph Poppen fell in love with the place. results.title: Online gambling, crypto bets draw more Korean soldiers into debt
results.content: “I’m currently a corporal and due to be discharged next June. I already owe around 20 million won ($15,000) to banks, savings banks and other lenders,” reads a November post by a Gyeonggi Province-based soldier on an online platform matching borrowers with private moneylenders. “Is there anywhere I could get my hands on 5 million won?” Such appeals are becoming harder to ignore as more young servicemen in Korea turn to high-interest lenders to finance online gambling and cryptocurrency investments. The problem has grown serious enough for financial authorities to move to curb a source of credit that many soldiers have come to rely on: personal loans from private lenders. results.title: YECCO students bring Korea's heritage to life with 'Histours' for foreign visitors
results.content: Where in the world can you get a professional-level, in-depth tour of an important monument or museum for free? Seoul, that’s where. And the Youth Exchanging Culture Communicators’ Organization (YECCO) is who. I recently joined them for a “Histour” of Gyeongbok Palace. The name signals the tour's focus on historical interpretation and information. The day was crisp, but bright and beautiful — perfect for exploring the nooks and crannies of the sprawling complex. My guides were YECCO President Kang Min-su and two very capable assistants, Kang Seo-hyun and Jeon Ju-hyeon. YECCO is a group of dynamic university students making a significant contribution to the city and nation by introducing Korea to the world. results.title: Korea's college entrance exam captures global interest again, this time over AI cheating crackdown
results.content: SEATTLE — South Korea's notoriously competitive college entrance exam has long fascinated international audiences for its grueling questions and the extraordinary measures the country takes to ensure a smooth testing environment. This year, however, the exam is drawing global attention for an entirely different reason: artificial intelligence (AI). As hundreds of thousands of students sit for the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), better known as Suneung, Thursday, people outside Korea are closely following the country's efforts to prevent AI-assisted cheating. results.title: Governments warn Java flaw leaves computer systems open to hackers
results.content: SEOUL/SHENZHEN — Governments around the world sounded the alarm on Wednesday over a critical flaw in the popular programming language Java that could allow hackers to access computer systems, the latest high-profile cyber incidentin recent weeks. U.S. tech firm Calif, which last month found a cybersecurity flaw in another programming language, PHP, said on Wednesday it had discovered the bug in Java's memory functions. The vulnerability could allow hackers to remotely execute code or to crash systems. U.S., South Korean, German and British authorities and China's Tencent urged companies and organisations to install a fix for the vulnerability, while the Dutch cybersecurity agency said it was investigating the issue. results.title: Historical epics return to Korean TV, led by 'Sword & Silence,' 'The Sacred Jewel'
results.content: Historical dramas are returning to the battlefield. Breaking away from a recent trend in which lighter genres such as romance and comedy dominated television, a series of big-budget productions depicting Korea’s struggles against foreign powers during the Silla and Goryeo periods are set to reach viewers toward the end of the year. Industry observers attribute the return of large-scale war dramas to growing demand for stories of conflict and survival amid an increasingly unsettled world, as well as lower production costs enabled by artificial intelligence (AI) technology and overseas distribution deals. KBS’ historical epic “Sword & Silence,” its first major historical drama in three years since “Korea-Khitan War,” depicts a turbulent seventh-century period when the Three Kingdoms were approaching the end of more than 600 years of warfare.
